Encode and decode text

Source: R/encode.R
naxp_encode.Rd

naxp_encode() encodes text using a naxp, and naxp_decode() decodes the encoded values back to the canonical form of the text.

Usage

naxp_encode(text, naxp)

naxp_decode(x, naxp = NULL)

Arguments

text

A character vector.

naxp

A naxp from naxp_parse(), a pattern string or a naxp_encoded vector, whose naxp is used. For naxp_decode(), it is needed only if x is not a naxp_encoded vector.

x

A naxp_encoded vector, or an integer or double vector of underlying encoded values. Underlying encoded values must be non-negative integers up to the naxp's maximum encoded value, or NA.

Value

  • naxp_encode(): a naxp_encoded vector the same length as text. If the elements of text are named then the same names are applied to the elements of the returned vector.

  • naxp_decode(): a character vector of the decoded text, the same length as x. Where a value is 0 or NA, the text is NA. If the elements of x are named then the same names are applied to the elements of the returned vector.

Details

Each text that a naxp accepts is encoded as an integer from 1 to the naxp's maximum encoded value. Several texts may share an encoded value (for instance, a postcode written with and without a space), but each encoded value decodes to exactly one canonical form.

Invalid text

Text that the naxp does not accept is invalid and is encoded as 0, as in every naxp library. The same applies to

  • NA, and

  • any text that is not ASCII, whatever its marked encoding.

Encoded values are never NA, although is.na() reports 0 as missing in a naxp_encoded vector.

naxp_decode() returns NA for 0. No string can represent 0, because a naxp may accept the empty string.

Storage

Encoded values are stored as

  • integer if the naxp's maximum encoded value is less than \(2^{31}\), or

  • double if it is in the range \(2^{31}\) to \(2^{53}\).

If the maximum encoded value is over \(2^{53}\), both functions raise an error, because a double cannot store every integer over \(2^{53}\) exactly.

See also

naxp_accepts() and naxp_canonical_form() to check text without encoding it.

Use naxp_encoded() to construct a naxp_encoded vector from its underlying values (e.g. when reading encoded values from a file or database).

Examples

postcode_naxp <- naxp_parse(r"(\9\9\9\9 \s!! \A\A)")

postcodes <- naxp_encode(c("1012AB", "1012 AB", "not a postcode"), postcode_naxp)
postcodes
#> <naxp_encoded[3]> \9\9\9\9 \s!! \A\A
#> [1] 1012 AB       1012 AB       <invalid (0)>
as.integer(postcodes)
#> [1] 684114 684114      0

naxp_decode(postcodes)
#> [1] "1012 AB" "1012 AB" NA       
naxp_decode(684114L, postcode_naxp)
#> [1] "1012 AB"
